title: Failure Modes of Interior-Point SDP Solvers on Moment–SOS Hierarchies

paper.title: Failure Modes of Interior-Point SDP Solvers on Moment–SOS Hierarchies
paper.abstract:
Abstract Standard semidefinite programming (SDP) solvers working in double precision can become
unreliable on difficult problems, even when their output appears plausible. We
study this issue for SDP problems arising from high-order moment-SOS
hierarchies. Three polynomial optimization problems are analysed by comparing
standard double-precision computations with reference solutions obtained
using the extended-precision solver Loraine 64x4 . We observe two
distinct patterns of numerical failure. In false convergence , the
computed bounds form a smooth sequence but approach the limit at the wrong
rate. In stagnation , the sequence develops a plateau or oscillations
and no longer reflects the convergence of the underlying hierarchy. We
introduce an empirical effective condition number based on the positive
spectral components of the primal and dual solution matrices. It serves as a
warning indicator rather than an error bound, and its growth accompanies
numerical deterioration in our examples. We also examine the imbalance
between primal and dual spectral conditioning and a Cholesky inverse residuum
as potential diagnostic indicators. The results show that solver termination
messages and apparently regular convergence curves may be insufficient to
establish the reliability of high-order moment-SOS bounds.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The moment-SOS hierarchy generates a sequence of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations whose optimal values converge to the global minimum of a polynomial optimization problem (POP) as the relaxation order ω \omega increases; see, e.g., Lasserre (2009) . Although some polynomial optimization problems admit finite convergence, the three problems studied here exhibit only asymptotic convergence. In finite precision, the higher-order relaxations can become increasingly ill-conditioned, and their numerical solution can lose accuracy. In this paper, we study two qualitatively different manifestations of this loss of accuracy. The first is false convergence : the computed relaxation values follow a smooth and apparently convincing convergence pattern, but with an incorrect asymptotic rate. The second is stagnation : the computed values cease to follow a systematic convergence trend and instead exhibit a plateau or oscillations. We analyse three polynomial optimization problems exhibiting these behaviours. Problems 1 and 2 show false convergence, while Problem 3 shows stagnation. Our analysis focuses on two distinct aspects of numerical accuracy. The first is the spectral conditioning of the primal and dual solution matrices, which affects the accuracy of the Newton step in an interior-point (IP) method. The second is the amplification of objective error when the optimal value is small. We quantify the latter effect by an objective amplification factor C C , defined in Section 3.5 . In our examples, this factor grows by several orders of magnitude with the relaxation order, so that even a modest error in the computed objective relative to the scale of the underlying matrices can result in a large relative error in the reported bound. To investigate the spectral conditioning, we analyse the Newton step of a primal-dual IP method, focusing on the formation and solution of the Schur complement system. This motivates the definition of the effective condition number κ eff = κ ⁡ ( X + ) ​ κ ​ ( S + ) , \kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}=\kappa(X_{+})\kappa(S_{+}), where X + X_{+} and S + S_{+} denote the restrictions of the exact primal and dual solution matrices to their positive eigenspaces. The product provides a heuristic measure of the combined precision demand associated with these spectral components. Its growth is associated with the observed deterioration in our examples, but, due to the limited number of problems studied, it should not be considered a general condition number. In numerical experiments, these condition numbers must be estimated from sufficiently accurate computed solutions. We also consider the ratio r = κ ⁡ ( S + ) κ ⁡ ( X + ) , r=\frac{\kappa(S_{+})}{\kappa(X_{+})}, which measures the imbalance between the dual and primal spectral conditioning. In our three examples, the false-convergence cases are strongly dual-dominated, whereas the stagnation case has comparable primal and dual factors. Of course, three examples are not enough to establish a general classification, but the pattern is worth noting. Computing these diagnostics reliably may require a high-precision solution, both to obtain accurate spectral information and to establish a trustworthy reference objective. These may not always be available or practical. We therefore also investigate a cheaper diagnostic that can be evaluated during the IP iteration: the Cholesky inverse residuum ρ = ‖ S ​ S comp − 1 − I ‖ , \rho=\|SS^{-1}_{\mathrm{comp}}-I\|, where S comp − 1 S^{-1}_{\mathrm{comp}} denotes the inverse action on S S computed using triangular solves, without forming an explicit inverse. In solvers that support multiple arithmetic precisions, monitoring ρ \rho may provide an early warning that higher precision is needed. The aim is to switch precision while the Schur complement matrix is still positive definite, rather than waiting for it to become indefinite. The appropriate threshold is solver- and problem-dependent, and ρ \rho does not monitor every source of numerical error. Numerical difficulties of SDP solvers on moment-SOS relaxations have been reported previously. Waki, Nakata and Muramatsu Waki et al. (2012) documented incorrect bounds, non-convergence, and other anomalous behaviour of interior-point methods applied to polynomial optimization, and studied the effect of extended-precision SDP solvers. The present paper sheds light on the numerical mechanisms behind false convergence and stagnation in our examples.

sections.heading: 2.1 Polynomial optimization and moment-SOS relaxations
sections.text: We first recall a primal-dual SDP pair in the sign convention used below: primal: max X ∈ 𝕊 m ⟨ B , X ⟩ subject to 𝒜 ∗ ​ ( X ) − c = 0 , X ⪰ 0 , dual: min y ∈ ℝ n , S ∈ 𝕊 m c T ​ y subject to 𝒜 ⁡ ( y ) − B − S = 0 , S ⪰ 0 . \begin{aligned} \text{primal:}\quad&\max_{X\in\mathbb{S}^{m}}&&\langle B,X\rangle\\ &\text{subject to}\ &&\mathcal{A}^{*}(X)-c=0,\\ &&&X\succeq 0,\end{aligned}\qquad\begin{aligned} \text{dual:}\quad&\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\,S\in\mathbb{S}^{m}}&&c^{T}y\\ &\text{subject to}\ &&\mathcal{A}(y)-B-S=0,\\ &&&S\succeq 0.\end{aligned} (1) Here, for any U , V ∈ 𝕊 m U,V\in\mathbb{S}^{m} , ⟨ U , V ⟩ = tr ⁡ ( U ​ V ) \langle U,V\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(UV) is the Frobenius inner product, 𝒜 ⁡ ( y ) = ∑ i y i ​ A i \mathcal{A}(y)=\sum_{i}y_{i}A_{i} , and 𝒜 ∗ ​ ( X ) i = ⟨ A i , X ⟩ \mathcal{A}^{*}(X)_{i}=\langle A_{i},X\rangle with A i ∈ 𝕊 m A_{i}\in\mathbb{S}^{m} , i = 1 , … , n i=1,\ldots,n . Note that in the actual moment-SOS formulations there can be several positive semidefinite constraints which, formally, can be written as 1 with block diagonal matrices X X and S S of the same block structure. With some abuse of notation, unless stated otherwise, in the text below X X and S S will only denote the principal Gram and moment blocks for which spectral data will be retained. The objective of polynomial optimization (POP) is to determine the optimal value f ∗ := min x ∈ ℝ ν ⁡ f 0 ​ ( x ) subject to f i ​ ( x ) ≥ 0 , i = 1 , … , μ , f^{*}:=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{\nu}}f_{0}(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_{i}(x)\geq 0,\ i=1,\ldots,\mu, where f 0 , … , f μ f_{0},\ldots,f_{\mu} are real polynomials. The moment-SOS hierarchy approximates f ∗ f^{*} from below by a sequence of SDPs indexed by the relaxation order ω \omega . The dual variable S S is a truncated moment matrix, together with a localizing matrix for each constraint f i f_{i} , while the primal variable X X consists of Gram matrices of an SOS certificate f 0 − f ω = σ 0 + ∑ i = 1 μ σ i ​ f i , f_{0}-f_{\omega}=\sigma_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{\mu}\sigma_{i}f_{i}, where σ 0 , … , σ μ \sigma_{0},\ldots,\sigma_{\mu} are SOS polynomials. The optimal value f ω f_{\omega} of the relaxation satisfies f ω ≤ f ∗ f_{\omega}\leq f^{*} for every ω \omega and, under standard assumptions, converges monotonically to f ∗ f^{*} as ω → ∞ \omega\to\infty . For details, see Lasserre (2015) ; Parrilo (2000) ; Nie (2023) . The problems studied below share two key features: – their optimal objective value is zero, and – the moment-SOS hierarchy does not attain this value at any finite relaxation order ω \omega . As ω \omega increases, the resulting sequence of SDPs grows in dimension, and its optimal values converge monotonically to zero without ever reaching it. Notice that the moment-SOS finite-convergence result requires standard nonlinear-programming conditions, LICQ, strict complementarity, and second-order sufficient conditions to be satisfied; see ( Lasserre, 2015 , Thm. 6.5) . Some of these conditions are violated in each of our problems. The examples below are taken from Baldi and Kočvara (2026) , where our primary interest was the rate of convergence. Numerical experiments aimed at estimating this rate revealed the stagnation and false convergence described above. In this article, we investigate these phenomena by comparing standard double-precision SDP solvers with the solver Loraine running in high-precision arithmetic.

sections.heading: 2.2 Solvers and reference computations
sections.text: To solve the resulting SDP problems, we use two popular SDP solvers, MOSEK MOSEK ApS (2025) and CSDP Borchers (1999) called through Julia/JuMP with their default settings. We compare their results with that of the high-precision Julia package Loraine.jl Habibi et al. (2024) 1 1 1 https://github.com/kocvara/Loraine.jl . Loraine relies on the extended-precision arithmetic provided by the Julia package MultiFloats.jl . In addition to the standard Float64 type, it defines types Float64x[N] with 𝙽 = 2 , … , 8 {\tt N}=2,\ldots,8 . For the purpose of this study, the values computed by Loraine running in Float64x4 extended precision are treated as the reference solution. Below we refer to this solver as Loraine 64x4 . The Loraine stopping criterion is based on the DIMACS error measures Mittelmann (2003) . sections.heading: 3.1 Positive spectral parts
sections.text: Let X X and S S denote the computed principal paired blocks from a Loraine reference run; i.e., the moment matrix ( S S ) and its dual Gram matrix. For a positive semidefinite matrix M M with eigendecomposition M = Q ​ Λ ​ Q T M=Q\Lambda Q^{T} , we define its numerically positive part by retaining the eigenvalues above the relative cutoff τ ⁡ ( M ) = 10 − 12 ​ λ max ​ ( M ) . \tau(M)=10^{-12}\lambda_{\max}(M). (8) Let Q + Q_{+} contains the corresponding eigenvectors; then we define M + = Q + T ​ M ​ Q + , κ ⁡ ( M + ) = λ max ​ ( M + ) λ min ​ ( M + ) . M_{+}=Q_{+}^{T}MQ_{+},\qquad\kappa(M_{+})=\frac{\lambda_{\max}(M_{+})}{\lambda_{\min}(M_{+})}. (9) The notation M + M_{+} denotes a restriction to a numerically selected subspace, not the usual projection of an indefinite matrix onto the PSD cone. Obviously, the full condition numbers of X X and S S are not useful for the purpose of measuring conditioning of the SDP problem. Along the central path, complementarity forces certain eigenvalues of X X and S S toward zero and so the full condition numbers of both matrices diverge as the barrier parameter decreases, even if the nonzero spectral clusters of the exact solution are well resolved. We therefore examine condition numbers of the restricted matrices X + X_{+} and S + S_{+} . This requires certain care as the numerical cutoff 8 does not always determine an exact rank. We use the spectra obtained by Loraine 64x4 with DIMACS tolerance 10 − 16 10^{-16} because the positive and near-zero clusters are visibly separated there and agree with still tighter runs in selected test cases. Changing the cutoff tolerance in 8 moderately leaves the reported ranks unchanged. For a fixed relaxation order, if the positive cluster of the exact solution is separated from zero and the computed matrix is sufficiently close in operator norm, standard invariant-subspace perturbation results imply stability of that cluster relative to the spectral gap ( Golub and Van Loan, 2013 , Thm. 8.1.10) . This supports the use of positive parts once two clusters are clearly resolved. It does not give a uniform guarantee along the hierarchy, because the gap separating the positive eigenvalues of the exact solution from zero may shrink with ω \omega .

sections.heading: 3.2 Numerical ranks and stopping tolerance
sections.text: The complete eigenvalue data for our three problems are given in Appendix 6 ; the main text uses only the quantities needed for the analysis. The computed spectra show that the routinely used DIMACS error tolerance need not ensure a reliable numerical rank. For Problem 2 at ω = 9 \omega=9 , for example, the numerical ranks of the computed X X and S S blocks change from 51 51 and 48 48 at tolerance 10 − 6 10^{-6} to 12 12 and 43 43 at tolerance 10 − 16 10^{-16} . For Problem 3 at ω = 6 \omega=6 , they change from 26 26 and 18 18 to 22 22 and 6 6 . In Problem 2, the numerical rank of S S is more stable under tolerance tightening than that of X X . In Problem 3, the rank of S S changes more substantially, while the rank of X X changes by four at each of the three orders considered. Several eigenvalues classified as positive in the lower-accuracy primal block move into the near-zero cluster in the tighter computation. Thus, numerical ranks inferred from a moderately accurate iterate can be misleading even when feasibility, gap, and complementarity residua appear satisfactory. sections.heading: 3.3 Numerical sensitivity of the Nesterov-Todd scaling
sections.text: In a primal-dual interior-point method, the Newton system couples the primal and dual semidefinite matrices through the linearized complementarity conditions. The Nesterov-Todd (NT) direction provides a symmetric primal-dual scaling for these conditions. Although we focus on NT scaling, the numerical difficulties associated with constructing the scaling and solving the resulting Newton system are not specific to this choice; other symmetric primal-dual scalings, such as the Helmberg-Kojima-Monteiro (HKM) scaling, also depend on the current primal and dual matrices and can exhibit similar sensitivity. The NT scaling matrix W ≻ 0 W\succ 0 is characterized by W ​ S ​ W = X . WSW=X. (11) Equivalently, W = X 1 / 2 ( X 1 / 2 S X 1 / 2 ) − 1 / 2 X 1 / 2 . W=X^{1/2}(X^{1/2}SX^{1/2})^{-1/2}X^{1/2}. (12) This scaling maps the primal and dual matrices to the same balanced matrix. Each Newton step of the IPM requires solving the Schur complement system M ​ Δ ​ y = h , M i ​ j = ⟨ A i , W ​ A j ​ W ⟩ . M\,\Delta y=h,\qquad M_{ij}=\langle A_{i},WA_{j}W\rangle. (13) The important point is that W W , and hence the Newton matrix M M , depends on both X X and S S . In Loraine, the NT scaling matrix W W is computed using Cholesky factorizations of the primal and dual matrices, followed by an SVD: X = L X ​ L X T , S = L S ​ L S T , X=L_{X}L_{X}^{T},\qquad S=L_{S}L_{S}^{T}, L S T ​ L X = U ​ Σ ​ V T . L_{S}^{T}L_{X}=U\Sigma V^{T}. The scaling matrix is then obtained as G = L X V Σ − 1 / 2 , W = G G T . G=L_{X}V\Sigma^{-1/2},\qquad W=GG^{T}. Thus, the computation of W W depends on both Cholesky factorizations and on the singular values in Σ \Sigma . In particular, small singular values are amplified by the inverse square root, making the accuracy of the computed scaling sensitive to the conditioning of the primal and dual matrices. Other symmetric directions, such as HKM, lead to different formulas but the same broad conclusion: the Newton equations inherit sensitivity from the current primal-dual matrices as well as from the problem data. It is useful to distinguish two computational stages: Stage 1: the scaling matrix W W is constructed and the Schur matrix M M is assembled; Stage 2: the Newton system 13 is solved. Numerical error can enter at both stages. Both depend on the primal and dual iterates, while the conditioning of the second stage also depends essentially on the data matrices A i A_{i} , their scaling, and their orientation relative to the eigenspaces of W W . Numerical safeguards such as regularization of a nearly singular Schur matrix and iterative refinement of the Newton direction address errors in Stage 2. They cannot, however, correct errors already introduced in Stage 1. In particular, if the conditioning of the positive spectral parts of X X and S S compromises the computation of W W , the resulting Schur matrix M M may be inaccurate, and solving the corresponding linear system accurately may still yield an inaccurate Newton direction.

sections.text: The preceding discussion motivates the definition of the effective condition number κ eff := κ ⁡ ( X + ) ​ κ ​ ( S + ) . \kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}:=\kappa(X_{+})\kappa(S_{+}). (14) We use κ eff \kappa_{\mathrm{eff}} as an empirical indicator of the combined conditioning of the selected primal and dual blocks. It does not account for the conditioning of the Schur system arising from the constraint matrices A i A_{i} and their interaction with the scaling matrix W W . It also omits the effect of the relative orientation of the relevant spectral subspaces, the barrier parameter, the remaining PSD blocks, and implementation-specific error propagation. The effective condition number can also be expressed in terms of the approximate number of decimal digits potentially lost to conditioning. For arithmetic carrying approximately p p decimal digits, this motivates the heuristic precision budget d heur = p − log 10 ⁡ κ ⁡ ( X + ) − log 10 ⁡ κ ⁡ ( S + ) = p − log 10 ⁡ κ eff . d_{\mathrm{heur}}=p-\log_{10}\kappa(X_{+})-\log_{10}\kappa(S_{+})=p-\log_{10}\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}. This expression estimates the number of decimal digits remaining after accounting for the conditioning represented by κ eff \kappa_{\mathrm{eff}} . It is not an estimate of the actual number of correct digits in the computed solution or objective, but a convenient way to compare the precision demands of different relaxation orders. For example, in double precision, with approximately p = 16 p=16 decimal digits, a target of seven digits corresponds to κ eff ≈ 10 9 \kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 10^{9} . sections.heading: 3.6 False convergence, stagnation, and spectral imbalance
sections.text: We define the spectral imbalance ratio r := κ ⁡ ( S + ) κ ⁡ ( X + ) . r:=\frac{\kappa(S_{+})}{\kappa(X_{+})}. (16) A large value of r r indicates that the selected dual block is much more ill-conditioned than the primal block. In our examples, this imbalance is associated with false convergence, whereas large values of κ eff \kappa_{\mathrm{eff}} , with comparable primal and dual condition numbers, are associated with stagnation; see Table 5 . Thus, r r provides a possible indicator of the type of numerical failure, rather than a criterion that defines or predicts it. For Problem 1, X + X_{+} is one-dimensional and κ ⁡ ( X + ) = 1 \kappa(X_{+})=1 , while κ ⁡ ( S + ) \kappa(S_{+}) grows rapidly. Problem 2 is also strongly dual-dominated over the displayed orders, although its primal block has increasing rank and its primal objective shows increasing numerical variability. Both problems exhibit a smooth but incorrect dual sequence. In Problem 3, the two positive-part condition numbers are comparable and both become large; the computed hierarchy loses its systematic trend and stagnates. These observations suggest that a large spectral imbalance ratio may serve as a warning sign for false convergence, while comparable primal and dual conditioning may accompany stagnation. However, three examples are far too few to establish this as a general principle. In particular, the ratio omits problem data and all other blocks, and Problem 1 does not separate the effect of a large ratio from the special fact that X + X_{+} has rank one.

sections.heading: 3.7 Cholesky inverse residuum
sections.text: The diagnostics discussed above rely on reliable spectral information about the primal and dual solutions or on a trusted reference objective value, which may require a high-precision computation. What can be monitored when only a standard solver is available, without an independent reference solution? We consider a simple diagnostic that can be evaluated during the interior-point iteration. A practical diagnostic available during an interior-point iteration is ρ := ‖ S ​ S comp − 1 − I ‖ , \rho:=\|SS^{-1}_{\mathrm{comp}}-I\|, (17) where S comp − 1 ​ v S^{-1}_{\mathrm{comp}}v denotes the inverse action obtained by solving with the computed Cholesky factors. No explicit inverse need be formed. The quantity measures the quality of this inverse action and uses the same factorization involved in constructing the NT scaling. For backward-stable factorization and triangular solves one expects the residuum to grow with machine precision and the conditioning of the full current iterate S S ; see ( Higham, 2002 , Thms. 10.3,10.4) . In the experiments, loss of useful progress was associated with values around 10 − 7 10^{-7} in Float64 and around 10 − 20 10^{-20} in Float64x4. These levels are empirical and solver-dependent; the latter is also influenced by the 10 − 16 10^{-16} stopping rule. The residuum is attractive because it is inexpensive and available during the solve. Its limitation is equally important: it monitors one factorization-based operation involving S S and contains no direct information about X X , the constraint operator, or objective amplification. It is a warning signal, not a universal stopping criterion. In solvers that support arithmetic at multiple precisions, the residuum ρ \rho could also serve as an early-warning indicator for switching to higher precision. Such a switch should be considered while the Schur matrix is still positive definite, rather than waiting for indefiniteness to occur, by which point numerical difficulties may already have compromised the iteration. The appropriate threshold for ρ \rho would need to be calibrated for the solver and problem class.

sections.heading: 3.8 Practical use of the diagnostics
sections.text: Table 7 summarizes the diagnostics in increasing order of availability in IP software, a short checklist for anyone computing moment-SOS bounds in finite precision. Table 7: Interpretation of the numerical diagnostics. Quantity Availability Main use Main limitation ρ \rho 17 during the solve warns of loss of accuracy in a Cholesky-based inverse action omits X X , constraint geometry, and objective amplification Primal-dual gap during the solve monitors agreement between the computed primal and dual objectives a small gap does not imply accurate objective values C C 15 with a trusted reference and block scale measures amplification of normalized objective discrepancy does not identify its source κ eff \kappa_{\mathrm{eff}} 14 after reliable spectral computation summarizes the positive-part spectral spread of the selected pair block- and representation-dependent; not an error bound r r 16 after reliable spectral computation describes primal-dual spectral imbalance no established classification role A reasonable workflow is therefore to monitor factorization residua during the solve, using the primal-dual gap as a measure of agreement between the computed objectives rather than as a certificate of their accuracy. One should inspect the hierarchy as a sequence rather than as isolated SDP runs, and use higher precision or independent references when the sequence becomes suspicious. A smooth curve is not by itself reassuring: it may be the signature of false convergence. Spectral diagnostics should be computed only from iterates accurate enough to separate positive and near-zero eigenvalue clusters.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusions
sections.text: The three examples demonstrate that numerical failure of successive SDP relaxations can produce two distinct patterns. In false convergence, the computed sequence of objective values remains smooth but follows the wrong asymptotic rate. In stagnation, it loses a systematic convergence trend and forms a plateau or oscillates. The first pattern is particularly dangerous because standard extrapolation can turn a numerical artefact into an apparently convincing convergence claim. Two effects should be kept separate. The objective amplification factor C C describes how a normalized discrepancy is magnified when the relaxation value approaches zero. Separately, the numerical analysis of the Newton step reveals a sensitivity to the conditioning of both the primal and dual semidefinite matrices. This motivates the effective condition number κ eff = κ ⁡ ( X + ) ​ κ ​ ( S + ) \kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}=\kappa(X_{+})\kappa(S_{+}) , which captures the combined spectral conditioning of the primal and dual solution components. Its growth is associated with the observed deterioration in our examples. However, given the limited number of examples studied, it should not be regarded as a general condition number of an SDP. The tolerance study gives a further warning: a small DIMACS error does not ensure that numerical ranks and positive-part condition numbers are already reliable. In Problems 2 and 3, tightening the tolerance changes the numerically identified primal positive subspace substantially. Spectral diagnostics therefore require sufficiently accurate iterates to separate positive and near-zero eigenvalue clusters; satisfying a standard stopping test may not suffice. The role of the imbalance ratio r = κ ⁡ ( S + ) / κ ⁡ ( X + ) r=\kappa(S_{+})/\kappa(X_{+}) is to organize the three examples: the false-convergence cases are strongly dual-dominated, whereas the stagnation case has comparable primal and dual factors. Although the pattern is consistent across these examples, its generality remains an open question. The Cholesky inverse residuum ρ \rho provides a cheap in-solver warning of loss of accuracy in the inverse action used to form the scaling matrix. In solvers supporting multiple arithmetic precisions, monitoring ρ \rho may help trigger a switch to higher precision before the Schur complement matrix becomes indefinite. The appropriate threshold is problem- and solver-dependent, and ρ \rho does not capture every source of numerical error. The central practical conclusion is that solver status, a small primal-dual gap, and a visually smooth sequence do not certify the accuracy of high-order moment-SOS bounds. The gap measures agreement between the computed primal and dual objectives, which may both be far from the true optimum. When the asymptotic behaviour matters, independent formulas, reliable spectral checks, alternative formulations, or higher-precision computations may be necessary. Related approaches include iterative refinement of approximate SDP solutions Mohammadisiahroudi et al. (2026) and rounding procedures that exploit an approximate optimal partition to construct an improved primal-dual solution Mohammad-Nezhad and Terlaky (2019) . Such methods provide possible routes to improving computed solutions, but their effectiveness for the high-order moment-SOS relaxations studied here remains to be investigated.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.17261v1 [math.OC] 12 Oct 2026 MSC Classification]90C22, 90C51, 65G50, 65F35 Failure Modes of Interior-Point SDP Solvers on Moment–SOS Hierarchies Michal Kočvara Email: m.kocvara@bham.ac.uk Affiliation: School of Mathematics, University of Birmingham, Birmingham, B15 2TT, United Kingdom Affiliation: Faculty of Civil Engineering, Czech Technical University in Prague, Thákurova 2077/7, Prague 6, 16629, Czech Republic Abstract Standard semidefinite programming (SDP) solvers working in double precision can become unreliable on difficult problems, even when their output appears plausible. We study this issue for SDP problems arising from high-order moment-SOS hierarchies. Three polynomial optimization problems are analysed by comparing standard double-precision computations with reference solutions obtained using the extended-precision solver Loraine 64x4 . We observe two distinct patterns of numerical failure. In false convergence , the computed bounds form a smooth sequence but approach the limit at the wrong rate. In stagnation , the sequence develops a plateau or oscillations and no longer reflects the convergence of the underlying hierarchy. We introduce an empirical effective condition number based on the positive spectral components of the primal and dual solution matrices. It serves as a warning indicator rather than an error bound, and its growth accompanies numerical deterioration in our examples. We also examine the imbalance between primal and dual spectral conditioning and a Cholesky inverse residuum as potential diagnostic indicators. The results show that solver termination messages and apparently regular convergence curves may be insufficient to establish the reliability of high-order moment-SOS bounds. keywords semidefinite programming, moment-SOS hierarchy, polynomial optimization, interior-point methods, condition number, extended-precision arithmetic pacs [ 1 Introduction The moment-SOS hierarchy generates a sequence of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations whose optimal values converge to the global minimum of a polynomial optimization problem (POP) as the relaxation order ω \omega increases; see, e.g., Lasserre (2009) . Although some polynomial optimization problems admit finite convergence, the three problems studied here exhibit only asymptotic convergence. In finite precision, the higher-order relaxations can become increasingly ill-conditioned, and their numerical solution can lose accuracy. In this paper, we study two qualitatively different manifestations of this loss of accuracy. The first is false convergence : the computed relaxation values follow a smooth and apparently convincing convergence pattern, but with an incorrect asymptotic rate. The second is stagnation : the computed values cease to follow a systematic convergence trend and instead exhibit a plateau or oscillations. We analyse three polynomial optimization problems exhibiting these behaviours. Problems 1 and 2 show false convergence, while Problem 3 shows stagnation. Our analysis focuses on two distinct aspects of numerical accuracy. The first is the spectral conditioning of the primal and dual solution matrices, which affects the accuracy of the Newton step in an interior-point (IP) method. The second is the amplification of objective error when the optimal value is small. We quantify the latter effect by an objective amplification factor C C , defined in Section 3.5 . In our examples, this factor grows by several orders of magnitude with the relaxation order, so that even a modest error in the computed objective relative to the scale of the underlying matrices can result in a large relative error in the reported bound. To investigate the spectral conditioning, we analyse the Newton step of a primal-dual IP method, focusing on the formation and solution of the Schur complement system. This motivates the definition of the effective condition number κ eff = κ ⁡ ( X + ) ​ κ ​ ( S + ) , \kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}=\kappa(X_{+})\kappa(S_{+}), where X + X_{+} and S + S_{+} denote the restrictions of the exact primal and dual solution matrices to their positive eigenspaces. The product provides a heuristic measure of the combined precision demand associated with these spectral components. Its growth is associated with the observed deterioration in our examples, but, due to the limited number of problems studied, it should not be considered a general condition number. In numerical experiments, these condition numbers must be estimated from sufficiently accurate computed solutions. We also consider the ratio r = κ ⁡ ( S + ) κ ⁡ ( X + ) , r=\frac{\kappa(S_{+})}{\kappa(X_{+})}, which measures the imbalance between the dual and primal spectral conditioning. In our three examples, the false-convergence cases are strongly dual-dominated, whereas the stagnation case has comparable primal and dual factors. Of course, three examples are not enough to establish a general classification, but the pattern is worth noting. Computing these diagnostics reliably may require a high-precision solution, both to obtain accurate spectral information and to establish a trustworthy reference objective. These may not always be available or practical. We therefore also investigate a cheaper diagnostic that can be evaluated during the IP iteration: the Cholesky inverse residuum ρ = ‖ S ​ S comp − 1 − I ‖ , \rho=\|SS^{-1}_{\mathrm{comp}}-I\|, where S comp − 1 S^{-1}_{\mathrm{comp}} denotes the inverse action on S S computed using triangular solves, without forming an explicit inverse. In solvers that support multiple arithmetic precisions, monitoring ρ \rho may provide an early warning that higher precision is needed. The aim is to switch precision while the Schur complement matrix is still positive definite, rather than waiting for it to become indefinite. The appropriate threshold is solver- and problem-dependent, and ρ \rho does not monitor every source of numerical error. Numerical difficulties of SDP solvers on moment-SOS relaxations have been reported previously. Waki, Nakata and Muramatsu Waki et al. (2012) documented incorrect bounds, non-convergence, and other anomalous behaviour of interior-point methods applied to polynomial optimization, and studied the effect of extended-precision SDP solvers. The present paper sheds light on the numerical mechanisms behind false convergence and stagnation in our examples. 2 Numerical observations 2.1 Polynomial optimization and moment-SOS relaxations We first recall a primal-dual SDP pair in the sign convention used below: primal: max X ∈ 𝕊 m ⟨ B , X ⟩ subject to 𝒜 ∗ ​ ( X ) − c = 0 , X ⪰ 0 , dual: min y ∈ ℝ n , S ∈ 𝕊 m c T ​ y subject to 𝒜 ⁡ ( y ) − B − S = 0 , S ⪰ 0 . \begin{aligned} \text{primal:}\quad&\max_{X\in\mathbb{S}^{m}}&&\langle B,X\rangle\\ &\text{subject to}\ &&\mathcal{A}^{*}(X)-c=0,\\ &&&X\succeq 0,\end{aligned}\qquad\begin{aligned} \text{dual:}\quad&\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\,S\in\mathbb{S}^{m}}&&c^{T}y\\ &\text{subject to}\ &&\mathcal{A}(y)-B-S=0,\\ &&&S\succeq 0.\end{aligned} (1) Here, for any U , V ∈ 𝕊 m U,V\in\mathbb{S}^{m} , ⟨ U , V ⟩ = tr ⁡ ( U ​ V ) \langle U,V\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(UV) is the Frobenius inner product, 𝒜 ⁡ ( y ) = ∑ i y i ​ A i \mathcal{A}(y)=\sum_{i}y_{i}A_{i} , and 𝒜 ∗ ​ ( X ) i = ⟨ A i , X ⟩ \mathcal{A}^{*}(X)_{i}=\langle A_{i},X\rangle with A i ∈ 𝕊 m A_{i}\in\mathbb{S}^{m} , i = 1 , … , n i=1,\ldots,n . With some abuse of notation, unless stated otherwise, in the text below X X and S S will only denote the principal Gram and moment blocks for which spectral data will be retained. The objective of polynomial optimization (POP) is to determine the optimal value f ∗ := min x ∈ ℝ ν ⁡ f 0 ​ ( x ) subject to f i ​ ( x ) ≥ 0 , i = 1 , … , μ , f^{*}:=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{\nu}}f_{0}(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_{i}(x)\geq 0,\ i=1,\ldots,\mu, where f 0 , … , f μ f_{0},\ldots,f_{\mu} are real polynomials. The moment-SOS hierarchy approximates f ∗ f^{*} from below by a sequence of SDPs indexed by the relaxation order ω \omega . The dual variable S S is a truncated moment matrix, together with a localizing matrix for each constraint f i f_{i} , while the primal variable X X consists of Gram matrices of an SOS certificate f 0 − f ω = σ 0 + ∑ i = 1 μ σ i ​ f i , f_{0}-f_{\omega}=\sigma_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{\mu}\sigma_{i}f_{i}, where σ 0 , … , σ μ \sigma_{0},\ldots,\sigma_{\mu} are SOS polynomials. The optimal value f ω f_{\omega} of the relaxation satisfies f ω ≤ f ∗ f_{\omega}\leq f^{*} for every ω \omega and, under standard assumptions, converges monotonically to f ∗ f^{*} as ω → ∞ \omega\to\infty . The problems studied below share two key features: – their optimal objective value is zero, and – the moment-SOS hierarchy does not attain this value at any finite relaxation order ω \omega . As ω \omega increases, the resulting sequence of SDPs grows in dimension, and its optimal values converge monotonically to zero without ever reaching it. Notice that the moment-SOS finite-convergence result requires standard nonlinear-programming conditions, LICQ, strict complementarity, and second-order sufficient conditions to be satisfied; see ( Lasserre, 2015 , Thm. 6.5) . Some of these conditions are violated in each of our problems. The examples below are taken from Baldi and Kočvara (2026) , where our primary interest was the rate of convergence. Numerical experiments aimed at estimating this rate revealed the stagnation and false convergence described above. In this article, we investigate these phenomena by comparing standard double-precision SDP solvers with the solver Loraine running in high-precision arithmetic. 2.2 Solvers and reference computations To solve the resulting SDP problems, we use two popular SDP solvers, MOSEK MOSEK ApS (2025) and CSDP Borchers (1999) called through Julia/JuMP with their default settings. We compare their results with that of the high-precision Julia package Loraine.jl Habibi et al. (2024) 1 1 1 https://github.com/kocvara/Loraine.jl .
